name: Rehoboam
bio:
Rehoboam was Solomon's son, who succeeded him as king after Solomon's forty-year reign ended and he was buried in the City of David (1 Kings 11:41-43).

Rehoboam went to Shechem, where all Israel had gathered to make him king. Jeroboam, recalled from his exile in Egypt, came with the assembly and asked Rehoboam to lighten the heavy labor and taxation Solomon had placed on the people, promising their loyalty in return. Rehoboam asked for three days to consider, then rejected the advice of Solomon's experienced elders — who urged him to serve the people and win them over with kind words — in favor of the advice of the young men he had grown up with, who told him to answer harshly: "My father scourged you with whips; I will scourge you with scorpions." When Rehoboam gave this harsh answer, the assembled Israelites abandoned him on the spot, crying, "What share do we have in David... To your tents, Israel!" — all but the tribe of Judah rejected his rule. When Rehoboam sent Adoram, in charge of the forced labor, to try to enforce his authority, all Israel stoned him to death, and Rehoboam himself barely escaped to Jerusalem by chariot (1 Kings 12:1-19). Back in Jerusalem, Rehoboam assembled 180,000 soldiers from Judah and Benjamin to force the northern tribes back under his rule, but the LORD sent Shemaiah the man of God to tell him not to fight his own brothers, since the division was the LORD's doing; Rehoboam obeyed and the armies stood down (1 Kings 12:21-24). Chronicles adds that Rehoboam then fortified fifteen cities across Judah and Benjamin, including Bethlehem, Hebron, and Lachish, stocking each with supplies, shields, and spears, and that priests and Levites streamed south to Judah from all over Israel because Jeroboam had cast them out of the priesthood in favor of priests of his own choosing for the high places and golden calves; for three years, as long as Judah walked in the ways of David and Solomon, the kingdom remained strong. Rehoboam married widely — eighteen wives and sixty concubines, fathering twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters — but loved Maachah, daughter of Absalom, above all the rest, and made her son Abijah chief among his brothers, intending him to be the next king (2 Chronicles 11:5-23). Rehoboam reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem; his mother was Naamah, an Ammonite. Under his rule, Judah did evil in the LORD's sight, building high places, sacred stones, and Asherah poles on every high hill, with even shrine prostitution appearing in the land. In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak, king of Egypt, attacked Jerusalem and carried off the treasures of both the temple and the royal palace, including all the gold shields Solomon had made; Rehoboam replaced them with bronze shields instead, carried by the palace guards whenever the king entered the temple. There was continual war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their reigns. When Rehoboam died, he was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Abijam succeeded him (1 Kings 14:21-31). Chronicles records his acts in the books of Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer on genealogies (2 Chronicles 12:15). His reign, which saw the kingdom torn in two just as the prophet Ahijah had foretold to Jeroboam, continues to unfold in detail in the chapters ahead.
